latin: Dīxitque Deus: “Fīat lūx.” Et facta est lūx.
translation: And God said, “Let there be light.” And light was made.
context: Jerome's Vulgate, made in Bethlehem around 400, became the Bible of the medieval West. Every monk who learned Latin met these words on day one.

teaching_value.notes: Perfect contrast of jussive subjunctive fīat vs perfect passive facta est from the same verb idea; -que enclitic; all words basic.

image.alt: Genesis frontispiece, Moutier-Grandval Bible (Tours, c. 830–40)

latin: In prīncipiō erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum.
translation: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
context: The opening of John's Gospel in Jerome's Latin. Medieval scribes often gave its first word a full-page decorated initial.

teaching_value.notes: Drills erat ×3, in + abl., apud + acc., and predicate nominative (Deus erat Verbum: word order ≠ subject). Highly repetitive = ideal reading.

image.alt: Book of Kells, fol. 292r: 'In principio erat verbum'

latin: Tolle, lege; tolle, lege.
translation: Pick up and read; pick up and read.
context: In a Milan garden in 386, Augustine heard a child chanting these words, opened Paul's letters, and was converted.

teaching_value.notes: Two 2nd-conjugation/3rd-conjugation singular imperatives; perfect first-imperative drill and memorable pattern for tolle/lege/scribe/ora.

image.alt: Benozzo Gozzoli, Augustine departing for Milan (San Gimignano fresco cycle)

latin: Semper aut discere aut docēre aut scrībere dulce habuī.
translation: I always found it sweet either to learn or to teach or to write.

teaching_value.notes: Three infinitives as neuter subjects/objects with dulce; aut … aut …; habuī perfect. The 3 core verbs of a scholar's life.

context: Bede describing his own life at the monastery of Jarrow, where he lived from age seven and wrote the first history of the English.

image.alt: Scribe at work, Codex Amiatinus (Bede's monastery, c. 700)

latin: Quod nunc es fueram, … et quod nunc ego sum, tūque futūrus eris.
translation: What you are now, I was … and what I am now, you too will be.

teaching_value.notes: Every tense of sum in one couplet: es / sum / fueram / futūrus eris. Relative quod as 'what'. Classic tomb formula.

context: Alcuin, Charlemagne's chief scholar, wrote his own epitaph speaking to passers-by: a common Roman tomb idea reused for a medieval abbot at Tours.
text_check: verified vs Latin Library (omits 'famosus in orbe, viator')

image.alt: Hrabanus Maurus presented by Alcuin, Fulda manuscript (c. 830)

latin: Pater noster, quī es in caelīs, sānctificētur nōmen tuum.
translation: Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name.
context: The Lord's Prayer: every medieval Christian, literate or not, knew it in Latin.

teaching_value.notes: Relative clause with 2sg es, jussive passive subjunctive; the most-recited Latin text of the Middle Ages.

image.alt: Lindisfarne Gospels, incipit of Matthew

latin: Fēcistī nōs ad tē, et inquiētum est cor nostrum, dōnec requiēscat in tē.
translation: You made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.
context: The first paragraph of Augustine's Confessions, written in North Africa c. 397, a prayer-autobiography that taught the West to write about the self.

teaching_value.notes: Perfect 2sg fēcistī, pronoun cases (nōs, tē acc./abl.), neuter adjective agreement with cor, dōnec + subjunctive. Short and core-heavy.

image.alt: Botticelli, St Augustine in his Study (c. 1480)

latin: Ōtiōsitās inimīca est animae.
translation: Idleness is the enemy of the soul.
context: Benedict's Rule organised monastic days into prayer, reading and manual work; it shaped Western monasteries for 1,500 years.

teaching_value.notes: inimīcus + dative is a reusable pattern (amīcus, similis, ūtilis + dat.). 4 words.

image.alt: Fra Angelico, St Benedict (Perugia Altarpiece)

latin: Obscultā, ō fīlī, praecepta magistrī, et inclīnā aurem cordis tuī.
translation: Listen, O son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart.
context: The first words of Benedict's Rule. Monks heard the Rule read aloud chapter by chapter every day.

teaching_value.notes: Two 1st-conj. imperatives, irregular vocative fīlī, double genitive (aurem cordis tuī).

image.alt: St Benedict delivering his Rule to his monks

latin: Glōria in altissimīs Deō, et in terrā pāx in hominibus bonae voluntātis.
translation: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among men of good will.
context: The angels' song at Christ's birth, later expanded into the Gloria of the Mass.

teaching_value.notes: Datives Deō / hominibus; ellipsis of est; in + abl.

image.alt: Annunciation to the Shepherds, Book of Hours leaf (Cleveland Museum of Art)

latin: Sērō tē amāvī, pulchritūdō tam antīqua et tam nova, sērō tē amāvī!
translation: Late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so new, late have I loved you!
context: Augustine's most quoted prayer, regretting the years he spent searching for God outside himself.

teaching_value.notes: amāvī perfect 1sg; vocative apposition; tam … et tam; antīqua/nova agreeing with feminine pulchritūdō (3rd decl.).

image.alt: Philippe de Champaigne, St Augustine

latin: Dā mihi castitātem et continentiam, sed nōlī modo.
translation: Give me chastity and self-control, but not yet.
context: Augustine admits that as a young man he prayed for self-control while secretly hoping God would wait.

teaching_value.notes: dā + dative mihi + accusatives; nōlī as negative command (pair with nōlī + infinitive). Funny, human, memorable.

image.alt: Benozzo Gozzoli, St Augustine teaching in Rome

latin: Dē profundīs clāmāvī ad tē, Domine.
translation: Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord.
context: A penitential psalm prayed for the dead throughout the Middle Ages.

teaching_value.notes: clāmāvī perfect; dē + abl.; vocative Domine.

image.alt: Utrecht Psalter (Carolingian, c. 830)

latin: Dubitandō quippe ad inquīsītiōnem venīmus; inquīrendō vēritātem percipimus.
translation: By doubting we come to inquiry; by inquiring we perceive the truth.
context: Abelard's 'Yes and No' set contradictory authorities side by side so students would reason them out—the seed of scholastic method.

teaching_value.notes: Gerund in ablative ×2, the clearest gerund demo possible; 1pl presents.

text_check: verified vs la.wikisource Sic et non prologue

image.alt: Charles Durupt, Héloïse and Abelard (19th c.)

latin: Diēs īrae, diēs illa, solvet saeclum in favīllā.
translation: Day of wrath, that day will dissolve the world in ashes.
context: A medieval hymn on the Last Judgement, sung in Requiem Masses for centuries and set by Mozart and Verdi.

teaching_value.notes: Future solvet; diēs feminine in this sense with illa; syncopated saeclum. Rhyme & trochees aid memory.

image.alt: Souls rising at the Last Judgement, Autun Cathedral tympanum

latin: Nūllus līber homo capiātur vel imprisonētur … nisi per lēgāle iūdicium parium suōrum vel per lēgem terrae.
translation: No free man shall be seized or imprisoned … except by the lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land.
context: King John sealed this charter at Runnymede in 1215. Clause 39 became a foundation of due process.

teaching_value.notes: Passive jussive subjunctives; nisi 'except'; legal Latin with medieval neologism imprisonetur (teach as such).

image.alt: Magna Carta 1215, British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106

latin: “Bene,” inquit; “nam et angelicam habent faciem.”
translation: “Good,” he said, “for they have the face of angels.”
context: Bede tells how Gregory the Great saw English slave boys in Rome, punned on Angli/angelī, and later sent missionaries to England (597).

teaching_value.notes: inquit for speech, present 3pl habent, adjective agreement. Pun Angli/angeli teaches vocab via story. Anecdote is Bede's report (traditional), text verified.

image.alt: St Petersburg Bede (8th c.), fol. 3v

latin: Vidēmus nunc per speculum in aenigmate, tunc autem faciē ad faciem.
translation: We see now through a mirror, in a riddle, but then face to face.
context: Paul's image of partial knowledge, read by medieval thinkers as a theory of how we know God.

teaching_value.notes: nunc … tunc contrast; per + acc.; fifth-declension faciēs in two cases.

text_check: verified vs drbo.org Clementine Vulgate 1 Cor 13:12 (Latin Library page didn't load)

image.alt: Rembrandt, St Paul at his writing desk

latin: Omnēs supervenientēs hospitēs tamquam Chrīstus suscipiantur.
translation: Let all guests who arrive be received as Christ.
context: Benedict's chapter on hospitality: monasteries became the inns, hospitals and schools of early medieval Europe.

teaching_value.notes: Jussive passive subjunctive (-antur) and present participle as adjective. Teaches a frequent 'rule-book' construction.

image.alt: Abbey of Monte Cassino, Benedict's monastery

latin: Tardiloquum tē esse iubeō.
translation: I order you to be slow to speak.
context: Advice on how to study, attributed to Aquinas in a short letter to a young friar named John.

teaching_value.notes: Textbook iubeō + acc. + infinitive; compound adjective. Letter's authenticity is doubted → traditional.

image.alt: Carlo Crivelli, St Thomas Aquinas

latin: Agnus Deī, quī tollis peccāta mundī, miserēre nōbīs.
translation: Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.
context: Pope Sergius I added this chant to the Mass around 700; it was sung daily in every church.

teaching_value.notes: Relative + 2sg verb, deponent imperative miserēre; tollis recalls 'tolle, lege'.

image.alt: Van Eyck, Ghent Altarpiece: Adoration of the Lamb (detail)

latin: Ō Fortūna, velut lūna statū variābilis, semper crēscis aut dēcrēscis.
translation: O Fortune, like the moon, changeable in state, you are always waxing or waning.
context: From a 13th-century songbook of wandering scholars, found at Benediktbeuern; Carl Orff set it to music in 1937.

teaching_value.notes: Vocative; 2sg presents crēscis/dēcrēscis; ablative of respect statū. Known from Orff.

text_check: verified vs Bibliotheca Augustana CB 17 and la.wikisource

image.alt: Wheel of Fortune, Codex Buranus (13th c.)

latin: Vānitās vānitātum, dīxit Ecclesiastēs, vānitās vānitātum; omnia vānitās.
translation: Vanity of vanities, said the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
context: The Preacher's refrain. Medieval and Baroque 'vanitas' paintings of skulls and candles took their name from it.

teaching_value.notes: 3rd-decl. nominative vs genitive plural of one noun; omnia neuter plural; dīxit perfect.

text_check: verified vs Latin Library Eccl. 1:2 (punctuation added)

image.alt: After Pieter Claesz, Vanitas still life (c. 1634)

latin: Ō quam citō trānsit glōria mundī.
translation: O how quickly the glory of the world passes away.
context: From The Imitation of Christ, the most-read devotional book of the late Middle Ages. The later papal formula 'Sic transit gloria mundi' echoes it.

teaching_value.notes: quam + adverb exclamation; citō; trānseō; genitive mundī.

image.alt: Portrait print of Thomas à Kempis (Rijksmuseum)

latin: Kārius mihi et dignius vidērētur tua dīcī meretrīx quam illīus imperātrīx.
translation: It would seem dearer and more honourable to me to be called your mistress than his empress.
context: Héloïse, one of the best-educated women in 12th-century France, writing to Abelard years after their secret marriage and separation.

teaching_value.notes: Comparatives cārius/dignius + quam; passive infinitive dīcī; rhyme meretrīx/imperātrīx aids memory. Intermediate.

image.alt: 19th-c. print of the tomb of Abelard and Héloïse

latin: Basilica sānctae Deī genitrīcis Aquisgrānī opere mīrābilī cōnstrūcta.
translation: The basilica of the holy Mother of God at Aachen, built with wonderful workmanship.
context: Einhard's biography of Charlemagne describes the emperor's building projects, including his octagonal chapel at Aachen.

teaching_value.notes: Locative Aquisgrānī, PPP cōnstrūcta, ablative of manner opere mīrābilī.

image.alt: Interior of Charlemagne's Palatine Chapel, Aachen

latin: Rotam volūbilī orbe versāmus.
translation: We turn the wheel in its spinning circle.
context: Boethius wrote while awaiting execution in 524; Lady Philosophy and Fortune's wheel became the Middle Ages' favourite image of chance.

teaching_value.notes: Fortune herself speaks; 1pl versāmus, abl. orbe. Pair with O Fortuna.

text_check: verified vs Bibliotheca Augustana 2 pr. 2.9 and Bibliotheca Polyglotta

image.alt: Boethius and Philosophy, Consolation manuscript of 1385

latin: …hūmānum genus optimē sē habēre cum ab ūnō regitur.
translation: …the human race is in the best condition when it is ruled by one.
context: Dante, exiled from Florence, argued in Latin for a universal emperor to keep peace in Christendom.

teaching_value.notes: Agent ab + abl. with passive regitur; optimē; sē habēre idiom.

text_check: verified vs Latin Library Mon. 1.14.11 (indirect statement after 'sequitur')

image.alt: Botticelli, portrait of Dante

latin: …adveniēns ūnus passerum domum citissimē pervolāverit…
translation: …a single sparrow, arriving, flies swiftly through the hall…
context: A counsellor of King Edwin compares human life to a sparrow flying through a warm feasting hall out of winter darkness.

teaching_value.notes: Short excerpt: ūnus passerum (partitive gen.), citissimē (superlative adv.). Intermediate; use as reading passage.

image.alt: St Petersburg Bede (8th c.), fol. 3v
